title: Arrival pattern classifier benchmark log (personal)
content:
Goal:
Run a small, repeatable benchmark to see whether a lightweight arrival-pattern classifier can be used at the front of the router to adapt batching timeouts and preemptive batching behavior. Key questions: does classification reduce p99 under bursty arrivals? does it reduce overall token-cost by improving batching efficiency?

Setup summary (synthetic):
- Model: LLaMA-2-like 13B quantized variant we use for staging (short-seq optimized).
- Hardware: single-node A100-80GB (dev pool) and separate run on 1xT4 (for low-tier comparison).
- Workload generator: local harness that supports mixed-arrival distributions (poisson, on-off burst with configurable burst qps, and periodic microbursts).
- Sequence lengths tested: 64 tokens (default), 512 tokens (long tail).
- Concurrency: single-tenant test client sending requests with 50 simulated clients.
- Baseline routing: static batching timeout 8ms, naive prefix caching enabled.
- Classifier: tiny LSTM-based classifier at router ingest (100ms training/heuristic) that labels requests as steady|microburst|burst-plateau based on 1s sliding window of arrival timestamps.
- Actuation: for microburst -> reduce batching timeout to 2ms and enable preemptive multiplexing; for plateau -> increase timeout to 20ms to favor larger batches; for steady -> keep 8ms.

Runs and metrics captured per run (scripted, 120s windows after warmup):
- QPS observed, average batch size, KV-cache hit rate, p50/p95/p99 latency (server-side), token cost delta (estimated), failed requests (timeouts), and change in tail-latency SLO violations (>800ms).

Key run IDs and short notes:
- run-A100-Poisson-64: baseline poisson (lambda=20 qps). Avg batch=3.2; p99=82ms; p95=44ms; p50=12ms; cache-hit=28%; SLO violations: 0.2%
- run-A100-Microburst-64-Baseline: on-off bursts (burst=120 qps for 200ms every 2s). Avg batch=2.4; p99=340ms; p95=150ms; p50=20ms; cache-hit=16%; SLO violations: 6.8%
- run-A100-Microburst-64-Classifier: same arrival pattern, classifier in-path. Avg batch=2.1; p99=180ms; p95=92ms; p50=18ms; cache-hit=15%; SLO violations: 1.9%
- run-A100-Plateau-512-Classifier: heavy sustained qps=40, long sequences. Avg batch=6.8; p99=520ms; p95=210ms; p50=96ms; cache-hit=52%; SLO violations: 3.1%
- run-T4-Microburst-64-Classifier: lower perf tier baseline vs classifier. p99 delta less pronounced but still ~25% improvement in p99.

Immediate observations:
- Classifier effectively cuts p99 in microburst patterns by ~40-50% relative to baseline on A100. The main mechanism seems to be aggressive timeout reduction + preemptive multiplexing that reduces queueing during 200ms bursts.
- Average batch size decreased slightly under classifier (expected), which nudged token-cost up by ~5% in the microburst scenario but reduced SLO violations substantially. Tradeoff: fewer costly SLO misses vs modest increase in unit cost.
- For steady/plateau patterns the classifier policy (increase timeout) recovered larger batch sizes and improved per-token efficiency without hurting p95 much.
- KV cache interactions: microburst observed lower cache-hit because bursts had many short unique prefixes; classifier doesn't materially change cache hit but reduced latency via faster dispatch.
- T4 runs show the same trend but magnitude of improvement on p99 is smaller (20-30%) and cost delta larger due to lower throughput efficiency.

Failure modes and caveats:
- Classifier mislabels during sudden changes (e.g., a long plateau that starts after a long quiet period) and the reactive policy can overshoot (increase timeout -> too-large batches -> spike when many short requests start). Need a dampening/backoff.
- Cold start: first 10s after deploy are noisy; warmup needed.
- Observability: router-level telemetry must expose sliding-window state to SLO dashboards so product owners can correlate classifier state with SLOs.
- Edge case: for long sequence workloads (512) classifier's timeout changes interact with token-level kernel scheduling, occasionally increasing p95 due to longer single-request compute times; consider sequence-length-aware policies.

Quick numbers table (derived):
- Microburst baseline p99: 340ms -> classifier p99: 180ms (47% reduction).
- Microburst token-cost delta: +5% (classifier).
- Plateau steady token-cost delta: -12% (larger timeout).

Next actions / experiments to run:
1) Add dampening: require two consecutive windows of same label before switching to a longer timeout (reduce oscillation).
2) Test classifier + sequence-length-aware policy: route long-seq to a separate pool or set per-request timeout heuristics.
3) Evaluate on multi-tenant noise: synthetic noisy tenant added to see cross-tenant classifier noise sensitivity.
4) Sweep classifier thresholds and measure false-positive/false-negative vs SLO benefit curve.
5) Instrument a small canary in staging for a week with detailed traces and integrate with alerting (SLO burn rate tied to classifier label).

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Might be worth a tiny feature in Optimize that suggests timeout profiles based on arrival distributions observed historically per-route.
- Consider combining classifier output with predictive queue-length estimator instead of raw labels for smoother actuation.
- If we go to production, we should add an opt-out per-tenant knob and a visible reason code whenever router changes timeout (for debugging).

References and links used in this log:
- github PR for the classifier prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482
- previous microburst experiments (Confluence): CONFLUENCE-RT-132

Short summary (1-2 lines): classifier-in-front-of-router has promising tail-latency benefits for short-seq microbursts at modest cost increase; next step is dampening and long-seq-aware policy before broader canary.

End of log.
